title: Xi and Modi Rebuild Ties as Two Asian Giants Seek Common Ground Before BRICS
excerpt: With Xi Jinping set to visit New Delhi for the BRICS summit this week, India and China are moving to repair a relationship damaged by border clashes and trade friction — driven by resumed flights, reopened trade crossings and a shared need to counter US tariff pressure.
body:
• Xi Jinping is expected to arrive in New Delhi on September 12 with a delegation of about 400 officials — his first visit to India in seven years — for the BRICS summit.
  • Bilateral trade hit a record $155 billion in 2023 and rose a further 23 per cent in the first seven months of 2024, even as India's trade deficit with China hovers near $100 billion.
  • India is considering easing restrictions on Chinese investment in manufacturing, renewable energy and auto components, while seeking greater access for Indian pharmaceuticals and IT services in China.
  • The diplomatic thaw accelerated after the 2024 border disengagement deal, the resumption of direct flights and the reopening of three Himalayan trade crossings this year.

Chinese President Xi Jinping's expected visit to New Delhi this week for the BRICS summit marks the most significant moment in India-China relations since a deadly border clash in 2020 drove the two countries apart. It will be Xi's first trip to India in seven years and only the third face-to-face meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi since the Galwan Valley confrontation that killed 20 Indian soldiers and at least four Chinese troops.

The visit comes against a backdrop of shifting global alignments. Both nations face steep tariffs from Washington — the United States raised duties on Indian goods to 50 per cent earlier this year — creating an opening for Beijing and New Delhi to explore common ground on trade and multilateral reform.

From Border Standoff to Diplomatic Reset

The relationship between the world's two most populous nations cratered after the June 2020 clashes along the Line of Actual Control in Ladakh. India banned dozens of Chinese apps, restricted Chinese investment and effectively froze high-level political contact for four years.

The turning point came in October 2024, when Modi and Xi met on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia — their first interaction since the crisis. That meeting produced a border disengagement agreement and set the stage for a broader diplomatic effort.

Since then, the two countries have agreed to resume patrols along their 3,500-kilometre border, restarted direct flights for the first time since 2020 and reopened border trade at three Himalayan crossings. India and China jointly organised a Hindu and Buddhist pilgrimage to sites in Tibet, and the long-suspended Kailash Mansarovar Yatra resumed.

"The interests of 2.8 billion people in both our countries are linked to our cooperation. This will also pave the way for the welfare of all humanity."

— Narendra Modi, at the SCO summit in Tianjin

Modi made the remark during bilateral talks with Xi on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin in August 2025, his first visit to China in seven years. Xi responded by calling for the "dragon and the elephant to dance together" and urged both sides to see each other as "development opportunities rather than threats."

Trade Recovery Meets Strategic Caution

The diplomatic thaw has been matched by a surge in commerce. Chinese customs data show bilateral trade rose 12.4 per cent in 2023 to a record $155 billion, with a further 23 per cent increase in the first seven months of 2024 compared to the same period a year earlier.

But the recovery is uneven. India's trade deficit with China reached nearly $100 billion in the 2024-25 fiscal year, with imports surging to $113.45 billion against exports of just $14.25 billion. New Delhi is pushing to rebalance the relationship by seeking greater market access in China for Indian pharmaceuticals, IT services and agricultural products.

India is also weighing a partial relaxation of the investment curbs imposed after the 2020 clashes. A proposal under consideration would allow Chinese investments of 20-25 per cent through the automatic route in sectors such as manufacturing, renewable energy and auto components, according to Mint. At the same time, India continues to restrict Chinese involvement in sensitive sectors like information technology.

Chinese companies including Envision, Geely-backed Horse Powertrain and CosMX have been exploring opportunities in India over the past 18 months, signalling renewed investment interest. However, Indian firms still face difficulties securing Chinese licences for rare earth magnets and industrial machinery, a source of friction that remains unresolved.

The US Tariff Factor

Washington's tariff actions have given both countries a reason to accelerate engagement. The 50 per cent US tariff on Indian goods, combined with ongoing trade tensions between Washington and Beijing, has created what analysts describe as a strategic opening.

During the Tianjin talks, Xi told Modi that "the international situation is both fluid and chaotic" and that India and China should be "partners who enable each other's success." Indian foreign secretary Vikram Misri said the two leaders explored ways to "leverage these global shifts to build greater understanding" and advance economic ties.

Both nations also called for reforms to the World Trade Organization and the multilateral financial architecture, arguing that existing institutions do not adequately reflect the economic weight of emerging economies.

What Comes Next in New Delhi

Xi's delegation to the BRICS summit is expected to include about 400 officials — more than double the size of his contingent during his last India visit in 2019, according to Reuters. Chinese officials are already finalising hotels and security protocols in New Delhi.

A bilateral meeting between Modi and Xi on the summit's sidelines is expected but not yet confirmed. The discussions are likely to cover border management, the trade deficit and potential expansion of Chinese investment in India.

Analysts caution that the rapprochement has clear limits. Praveen Donthi of the International Crisis Group notes that multilateral forums like BRICS provide a platform to manage differences but cannot resolve the deep structural trust deficit between the two countries. Amitabh Kant has said a thaw has begun, but rebuilding confidence will take time.

For now, the direction is unmistakable: two nations representing 2.8 billion people are choosing engagement over confrontation, even if the road to genuine trust remains long.
image_caption: Chinese President Xi Jinping meets Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Tianjin during the SCO summit in August 2025. Xi is expected to visit New Delhi this week for the BRICS summit, his first trip to India in seven years.
nri_angle: The India-China diplomatic reset has direct implications for the Indian diaspora, as trade policies, investment flows and geopolitical alignment between the two Asian giants shape economic opportunities and strategic positioning for Indians worldwide.
author: Diaspora Desk
